svg.title: RB2.1.1 — Component ID with EF 3.1 recovery priority
svg.desc: Component ID sub-tab: the NX drawing above, and below it a material list beside a horizontal chart plotting each material’s share of the minerals-and-metals impact against its Scenario 4 recovery rate.
svg.text: priority = mass x EF 3.1 ADP · LOG scale, 1e-6 to 100 %
THE ANSWER IS YES, and the factors came out of YOUR OWN method pack - openLCA LCIA Methods 2.4.0, "EF 3.1 Method (adapted)",
category b2ad6494-c78d-11e6-9d9d-cec0c932ce01 "Resource use minerals and metals", 170 factors, unit kg Sb eq. Nothing here is from memory.
ADP (ultimate reserves), kg Sb eq per kg: Gold 52.0 Silver 1.18 Antimony 1.0 (reference) Palladium 0.571 Tin 0.0162
Copper 1.37e-3 Nickel 6.53e-5 Tantalum 4.06e-5 Iron 5.24e-8 Aluminium 1.09e-9 Silicon 1.4e-11
CONNECTOR, priority = mass x ADP: Gold 0.04 % of mass -> 98.49 % of the impact. Aluminium 63.3 % of mass -> 0.000003 %.
Per gram, gold matters 4.8e10 times more than aluminium for this indicator. That is the single most useful sentence this tab can tell a recycler,
and it inverts what the mass list says. A pie chart of mass would have shown the exact opposite priority.
WHY A LOG AXIS: the shares span 98 % down to 3e-6 %. On a linear axis only gold would be visible and the chart would say nothing about the rest.
STILL NOT SOURCED - the Sc4 recovery rates. Gold 62.9 %, Nickel 72.5 %, Tin 40.2 % are [L] Lee 2012 via BOM_v4. Copper 85 % and Aluminium 90 %
are marked [A] and remain mine. The one that matters most (gold) is sourced, so the headline is defensible even if the [A] rows are not yet.
CAVEAT FOR THE THESIS: this is mass x characterisation factor, NOT an openLCA contribution result. It ignores ore grade, process losses and the
market processes your model actually uses, so call it a RECOVERY PRIORITY INDICATOR, not the study’s per-material impact. A contribution
analysis on this indicator would give the rigorous version - and would very likely rank gold first anyway.
